sources.source: Apache Kafka source, storage/internals/log module (read, not quoted)

items.item: a segment is really three files: the .log data file, a sparse .index offset file, and a .timeindex timestamp file

at.step: Setup: a partition is files on disk

items.item: A partition is a directory of segment files; only one segment (the active one) is open for appends at a time.

at.step: Setup: a partition is files on disk

items.item: Within a segment, the .log file holds the records; a parallel .index file holds a sparse offset-to-byte-position map and a .timeindex file holds a sparse timestamp-to-offset map.

at.step: Setup: a partition is files on disk

items.item: The index is sparse because Kafka only needs to narrow a seek down to roughly the right position, then finish with a short local scan — not locate every record by direct lookup.

at.step: Reveal: the offset index is sparse

items.item: A segment rolls to a new file once it crosses its configured size (or time) limit; the active segment is never eligible for compaction.

at.step: Reveal: the active segment rolls

items.item: Reads are served from the OS page cache, not a Kafka-managed in-process cache, by deliberate design choice.

at.step: Reveal: reads come from the page cache, with zero copies to spare

items.item: sendfile lets the broker hand the kernel a file descriptor so bytes move pagecache to NIC directly, skipping the extra kernel-to-user-to-kernel round trip a naive read/write loop pays.

at.step: Reveal: reads come from the page cache, with zero copies to spare

items.item: The zero-copy optimization compounds with multiple consumers: the same cached bytes serve every reader of that region, not a fresh copy per reader.
Kafka deliberately does not track per-consumer, per-record consumption state on the broker; a consumer's position is a single integer it owns and checkpoints itself.

at.step: Reveal: an offset belongs to the consumer, not the broker

items.item: Because the broker holds no per-record consumption state, a consumer can rewind to an old offset and re-read, which plain queue semantics don't allow.

at.step: Reveal: an offset belongs to the consumer, not the broker

items.item: sendfile/zero-copy is not used once TLS is enabled, a real, named operational cost of turning on encryption.
Log compaction physically rewrites segments out of append order, which is why it needs its own later topic (retention and compaction) rather than being folded into this one.
This topic is the entry point to the whole chapter; every later topic in 9.1-9.3 assumes the reader already has the partition/segment/offset vocabulary this topic introduces.
